concepts.title: application.properties, application.yml, and Property Precedence
concepts.description: Spring Boot reads configuration from a strict, ordered set of sources -- command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files, application.properties/yml, and more -- merging them into one unified Environment, and knowing that precedence order is exactly what lets you predict which value actually wins when the same property is set in more than one place.
learningObjectives: Write equivalent configuration in application.properties and application.yml and explain the structural difference between flat dot-notation keys and nested YAML mappings.
Explain what the Environment abstraction is and how it presents multiple underlying property sources as one queryable view.
List the most commonly encountered property sources in their relative order of precedence.
Predict which value wins when the same property is set in both application.properties and as a command-line argument.
Explain why YAML's indentation sensitivity is a common source of silent misconfiguration compared to the flatter .properties format.
Explain relaxed binding and why an environment variable like ORDER_SERVICE_URL can satisfy a property key named order-service.url.

sections.heading: Two File Formats, One Underlying Model
sections.body:
`application.properties` represents configuration as flat, dot-notation key-value pairs, one per line:

```properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
app.notifications.retry-count=3
```

`application.yml` represents the same information as a nested mapping, where indentation encodes the hierarchy that `.properties` spells out explicitly with dots:

```yaml
server:
  port: 8081
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
    username: orders_app
app:
  notifications:
    retry-count: 3
```

Both are read from the same place by default (typically `src/main/resources`), both flow into the exact same underlying configuration model once parsed, and Spring Boot supports either one -- but if both `application.properties` and `application.yml` are present in the same location at once, `.properties` takes precedence for any key they both define, which is a genuinely confusing situation worth avoiding altogether by picking one format per project rather than mixing them. YAML's appeal is real for deeply nested configuration (it avoids repeating a long common prefix on every line), but that nesting is also YAML's biggest practical hazard: whitespace and indentation are *structurally significant*, not stylistic. Two spaces of accidental extra or missing indentation doesn't produce a parse error the way a genuinely malformed line usually would -- it silently changes which parent a key nests under, producing a property that binds to the wrong place, or nowhere at all, with no warning.

sections.heading: The Environment Abstraction: One Queryable View Over Many Sources
sections.body: Spring Boot doesn't read `application.properties` (or `.yml`) directly and treat it as the single source of truth. Instead, every configuration source -- the properties file, environment variables, command-line arguments, and several others -- is registered as a `PropertySource` inside a single `Environment` object, and every mechanism that reads configuration (`@Value`, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and every autoconfiguration class discussed in the Core Concepts module) reads through that one `Environment`, never directly from any individual file or source. Calling `environment.getProperty("server.port")` walks the ordered list of registered `PropertySource`s and returns the value from the *first* one that actually defines that key -- which is the entire mechanism behind precedence: it isn't that lower-priority sources are ignored, it's that the `Environment` simply stops looking once it finds a match in a higher-priority source. This single point of unification is exactly why a component reading `spring.datasource.url` never needs to know or care whether that value ultimately came from a file, an environment variable, or a command-line flag -- from its point of view, there's just one `Environment`, with one value for that key.

sections.heading: Precedence Order: What Wins When Two Sources Disagree
sections.body:
Spring Boot's full, official precedence list runs to well over a dozen distinct source types (devtools-specific properties, test-context properties, `@TestPropertySource`, and more among them), but the subset that matters for almost all everyday development, from highest to lowest precedence, is:

1. Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`)
2. Java System properties (`-Dserver.port=9090`) and OS environment variables (roughly equal precedence, with command-line args still ranking above both)
3. Profile-specific files, `application-{profile}.properties`/`.yml` (covered fully in the Profiles concept later in this module)
4. The base `application.properties`/`.yml`
5. `@PropertySource`-referenced files and any hardcoded defaults in `@ConfigurationProperties` classes

The design intent behind this ordering is worth stating explicitly, because it explains *why* the list is shaped this way rather than the reverse: sources further up the list are progressively more specific to a particular deployment or a particular run, while sources further down are progressively more generic and baked into the build itself. A value baked into `application.properties` at build time represents 'the sensible default for this application in general'; a command-line argument or environment variable supplied at the moment a specific container starts represents 'what this particular running instance, in this particular environment, actually needs right now' -- and it should be able to override the generic default without anyone recompiling or repackaging anything. This is the exact mechanism, in fact, that the Core Concepts module already leaned on without spelling out the full ordering: `server.port=8081` in `application.properties` changing the embedded server's port works because `ServerProperties` reads through this same `Environment`, and everything from this section forward is just naming, precisely, the layered structure that made that single example work.

sections.heading: Relaxed Binding: Why Environment Variables Don't Need to Match the Property Key Exactly
sections.body:
A property key like `order-service.url` is a perfectly normal thing to write in `application.properties`, but it is *not* something you can reliably set as a literal environment variable name -- most shells either forbid dots and hyphens in environment variable names outright, or handle them so inconsistently across operating systems that relying on it would be fragile at best. Spring Boot solves this with **relaxed binding**: when resolving a configuration key, it doesn't require an exact character-for-character match against an environment variable's name. It normalizes both sides -- treating case differences, hyphens, underscores, and the dot/underscore boundary as equivalent -- so an environment variable named `ORDER_SERVICE_URL` is recognized as satisfying the property key `order-service.url` without any special mapping code or explicit aliasing written anywhere.

This exists for an entirely practical, operational reason: infrastructure and deployment tooling (Docker, Kubernetes manifests, CI/CD pipelines) overwhelmingly passes configuration through environment variables, in `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, because that's the one format essentially every shell and container runtime handles predictably. Relaxed binding is what lets an ops team override `order-service.url` -- or any other property, no matter how it's spelled in the properties file -- from a container's environment variables with zero special syntax or code changes, while application code and `application.properties` both keep using whatever naming convention (typically kebab-case or camelCase) reads best in that context.

examples.title: The Same Configuration in .properties and .yml
examples.code:
# application.properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
app.notifications.retry-count=3

# ---
# application.yml (equivalent, nested instead of dot-separated)
# server:
#   port: 8081
# spring:
#   datasource:
#     url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
#     username: orders_app
# app:
#   notifications:
#     retry-count: 3
examples.explanation: Every dot in the .properties keys corresponds to one level of nesting in the .yml version -- spring.datasource.url becomes spring: / datasource: / url: three levels deep. Both formats produce the exact same set of resolved key-value pairs once Spring Boot parses them into the Environment; nothing about which format you choose changes what @ConfigurationProperties classes or @Value placeholders end up seeing. The practical tradeoff is purely about readability and risk: .yml avoids repeating spring.datasource. on every line once you have many keys under one prefix, at the cost of every line's meaning depending on exactly how many spaces of indentation it has -- a risk .properties's flat, fully-spelled-out keys simply don't carry.

examples.title: Command-Line Arguments Overriding a File-Based Default
examples.code:
# application.properties, committed to the repository
server.port=8080

# Deployment / local override, with no code or file changes:
# java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
#
# Application actually starts listening on port 9090, not 8080.
examples.explanation: server.port=8080 in application.properties establishes the generic default baked into the build. Passing --server.port=9090 as a command-line argument registers a PropertySource with strictly higher precedence than the properties file, and because the Environment resolves a key by returning the value from the FIRST source (in precedence order) that defines it, the command-line value wins outright -- the properties file's value for that same key is simply never reached during resolution, not overwritten or deleted, just shadowed by a higher-precedence source for as long as that argument is supplied. This is exactly the mechanism that lets the identical jar file run on 8080 in one environment and 9090 in another with zero rebuilding.

examples.title: Relaxed Binding: An Environment Variable Satisfying a Kebab-Case Property
examples.code:
# application.properties
order-service.url=http://localhost:8082

# Container environment variable (typical Docker/Kubernetes style):
# ORDER_SERVICE_URL=https://orders.internal.example.com
#
# A component reading order-service.url via @Value or @ConfigurationProperties
# resolves to https://orders.internal.example.com when this env var is present --
# no explicit mapping between the two names was written anywhere.
examples.explanation: order-service.url and ORDER_SERVICE_URL look nothing alike character-for-character, but Spring Boot's relaxed binding rules normalize case, hyphens, underscores, and the dot/underscore boundary when matching a property key against an environment variable name, treating the two as referring to the same logical configuration value. Because environment variables (the format virtually every container platform and CI pipeline uses to inject configuration) rank above application.properties in precedence, setting ORDER_SERVICE_URL in a container's environment silently overrides the file-based default the moment that container starts -- with the file's kebab-case key never needing to change to accommodate it.

misconceptions.description: If a property is set in application.properties, that's the final, authoritative value -- command-line arguments or environment variables are only useful for setting values that AREN'T already in the file.
misconceptions.clarification: application.properties sits relatively low in Spring Boot's precedence order, specifically so that more deployment-specific sources -- command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files -- can override it. A property defined in BOTH the file and a higher-precedence source doesn't cause a conflict or an error; the higher-precedence source's value simply wins, with the file's value never actually being read for that key on that particular run. This is a deliberate design, not an edge case: it's exactly what lets the same built artifact behave differently across environments (different database URLs, different ports, different feature flags) without ever touching or rebuilding application.properties itself.

misconceptions.description: YAML and .properties are just two interchangeable syntaxes for writing the exact same file -- indentation in YAML is a style preference, similar to code formatting, not something that changes the file's meaning.
misconceptions.clarification: YAML's indentation is structurally significant, not cosmetic -- it's literally how the format encodes nesting, since there are no dots or braces doing that job the way there are in .properties or JSON. Shifting a key one space to the left or right can silently move it to a different level of nesting entirely, producing a property that binds under the wrong parent key (or under no meaningful parent at all) -- and this typically produces no parse error, just a configuration value that's quietly never applied, which is a substantially harder class of bug to notice than a plainly mistyped key in a flat .properties file.

exercises.prompt: Given an application.properties file containing `server.port=8080`, the application is started with the command `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090`. What port does the embedded server actually listen on, and why?
exercises.code:
# application.properties
server.port=8080

# Startup command:
# java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
hints: Command-line arguments and application.properties are two separate PropertySources inside the same Environment -- which one has higher precedence?
The Environment resolves a key by returning the value from the FIRST source, in precedence order, that defines it -- it doesn't merge or average conflicting values.
Nothing about the file itself changes; the file's value for server.port is simply never reached during resolution on this particular run.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 9090. Command-line arguments rank above application.properties in Spring Boot's property source precedence, so the Environment resolves server.port to the command-line value; application.properties's value of 8080 is shadowed for this run, not overwritten in the file itself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both the command-line argument and the properties file register a value for the same key, server.port, as two separate PropertySources inside the application's single Environment. Command-line arguments sit at the top of Spring Boot's precedence order, above application.properties, so when anything -- in this case, the autoconfiguration responsible for the embedded server -- asks the Environment for server.port, it returns the first value found while walking sources in precedence order, which is the command-line argument's 9090. application.properties's own value of 8080 is never actually consulted for this particular run; the file itself is completely unchanged, and starting the same jar again WITHOUT the --server.port argument would correctly fall back to reading 8080 from the file, since nothing above it in precedence would define the key in that case.

exercises.prompt: A developer expects app.notifications.retry-count to be nested under app.notifications, but @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notifications") always reports retryCount as its default value of 1, never the 5 from this file. Find and fix the YAML indentation bug.
hints: Compare the indentation level of retry-count and channel against the indentation level of notifications directly above them.

In YAML, a key nests under whichever key directly above it has LESS indentation and ends with a colon -- retry-count and channel here are at the exact same indentation as notifications, not one level deeper.
Indent retry-count and channel two more spaces than notifications so they become children of it, rather than unrelated siblings at the same level as notifications itself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the buggy version, notifications: has no keys indented further than itself -- retry-count and channel sit at the SAME indentation level as notifications, which YAML interprets as them being siblings of notifications under app, not children of it. That silently produces a property path of app.retry-count (not app.notifications.retry-count), which @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notifications") never looks at, so its retryCount field is left at whatever default was set in the Java class, 1 -- with no parsing error anywhere, since app.retry-count is itself perfectly valid YAML, just bound to the wrong logical location. Indenting retry-count and channel two spaces further than notifications makes them genuinely nest underneath it, producing the intended app.notifications.retry-count path that the @ConfigurationProperties class is actually configured to read from.

assessments.prompt: A property is defined in both an OS environment variable and application.properties, with different values. Which value does Spring Boot's Environment resolve to?
options: application.properties always wins, because it's explicitly part of the application's own packaged configuration.
The environment variable's value wins, because OS environment variables rank above application.properties in Spring Boot's property source precedence order.
Spring Boot throws a startup exception because the same property is defined in two conflicting places.
Whichever source was read first at startup wins, which is effectively random.
assessments.explanation: OS environment variables sit above application.properties in Spring Boot's precedence order specifically because they represent deployment-time, environment-specific configuration meant to be able to override generic, build-time defaults -- so the Environment resolves to the environment variable's value. Option A inverts the actual precedence. Option C is wrong -- having the same key defined in multiple sources is completely normal and expected, precisely because overriding is the intended use case, not an error condition. Option D is wrong -- resolution follows a fixed, documented, deterministic precedence order, not source-read timing.

assessments.prompt: A teammate maintains three separate copies of application.properties -- one per environment -- and manually swaps the right one into the build before each deployment. Explain, using the Environment and precedence concepts, a better approach that avoids maintaining multiple property files by hand.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core problem with maintaining three separate application.properties files is that it ties environment-specific values (database URLs, feature flags, ports) to which FILE gets built into the artifact, which means the artifact itself is different per environment -- you're not really deploying 'the app' three times, you're building and deploying three subtly different apps, and it's easy for the files to drift out of sync with each other over time. The better approach leans on the fact that Spring Boot's Environment merges many property sources into one queryable view, with a well-defined precedence order, rather than treating application.properties as the sole source of truth. Instead of three files, you'd keep ONE application.properties containing only the values that are genuinely the same everywhere (or sensible generic defaults), and supply everything that's actually environment-specific -- the database URL, an API key, a feature flag -- through a higher-precedence source at deploy time: OS environment variables set in the container/orchestration platform, or command-line arguments passed to the same jar. Because environment variables and command-line arguments both rank above application.properties in the resolution order, the SAME built jar, unchanged, picks up different values for those keys purely based on what the deployment environment supplies at startup -- there's no need to rebuild, no need to swap files, and no risk of the three files silently drifting apart, because there's only one file (plus, in more elaborate setups, profile-specific overlay files, covered in a later concept in this module) instead of three independently-maintained ones.

concepts.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties
concepts.description: @Value pulls in one property at a time through a placeholder expression, while @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole group of related keys onto a strongly-typed, optionally validated class -- and picking the wrong one for a given job trades away either simplicity or the fail-fast safety that grouped, validated configuration classes give you almost for free.
learningObjectives: Inject a single scalar property with @Value, including the ${property.key:defaultValue} placeholder syntax.
Bind a group of related properties into a strongly-typed class using @ConfigurationProperties and a prefix.
Explain why an @ConfigurationProperties class needs to be registered as a bean via @Component, @EnableConfigurationProperties, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan before binding actually happens.
Explain constructor binding for an immutable @ConfigurationProperties class and why it's preferred over mutable setter binding.
Explain why @ConfigurationProperties classes can be validated with @Validated and JSR-380 constraint annotations in a way plain @Value usage generally isn't.
Predict the difference in failure behavior between a typo'd property key used with @Value and one used with a validated @ConfigurationProperties class.

sections.heading: @Value: One Property at a Time, Inline
@ConfigurationProperties: Binding a Whole Group as One Object
Constructor Binding for Immutability
Validation and Fail-Fast Configuration

examples.title: @Value With and Without a Default
examples.explanation: retryCount has a default of 3, so a missing app.notifications.retry-count property resolves quietly to that fallback, with no error of any kind -- appropriate when a sensible default genuinely exists. channel has no default at all, which is a deliberate choice for a property with no reasonable fallback value: if it's missing everywhere, Spring throws an exception during placeholder resolution rather than injecting null, failing the whole application startup immediately instead of letting a NotificationClient silently exist with a channel that's never actually set. The tradeoff to notice is that this fail-fast behavior only applies to properties WITHOUT a default -- add a default to channel and a typo'd real property key would once again fail completely silently, always falling back to that default.

examples.title: A Registered, Grouped @ConfigurationProperties Class
examples.explanation: @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class is what actually registers NotificationProperties as a bean -- without it (and without an alternative like @Component on the class itself, or @EnableConfigurationProperties elsewhere), NotificationProperties would never be bound to real configuration at all, and every field would silently stay at its hardcoded Java default of 3 and "email" forever, regardless of what app.notifications.retry-count or app.notifications.channel actually say in application.properties. Once properly registered, NotificationService receives the fully-bound NotificationProperties bean through ordinary constructor injection, exactly like any other dependency -- grouping app.notifications.retry-count and app.notifications.channel behind one typed object, rather than two separate @Value fields scattered wherever they're individually needed.

examples.title: Constructor Binding With Validation, Failing Fast on Bad Config
examples.explanation: Because NotificationProperties has exactly one constructor, Spring Boot uses it automatically for constructor binding -- both fields are final and populated in one atomic construction step, with no mutable intermediate state. @Validated tells Spring Boot to run Bean Validation against the fully-bound object immediately after construction, checking channel against @NotBlank and retryCount against @Min(0). With the shown (deliberately invalid) configuration, both constraints fail, and the application refuses to start at all, printing exactly which fields failed and why -- catching a bad deployment configuration at the moment the container boots, rather than only surfacing as a mysterious runtime failure the first time some code path actually tries to use an empty channel or a negative retry count.

misconceptions.description: @Value("${some.key:default}") is just as safe as a strongly-typed, validated @ConfigurationProperties class -- if the real property key is ever typo'd elsewhere in configuration, at least there's a default, so nothing actually breaks.
misconceptions.clarification: That silent fallback is exactly the danger, not a safety net: a typo'd real property key with a default supplied via @Value produces no error, no warning, and no visible signal anywhere that the intended override was never applied -- the application just always uses the default, indefinitely, looking completely healthy while quietly running with the wrong configuration. A validated @ConfigurationProperties class doesn't have this blind spot in the same way, both because grouping related keys under one prefix makes it easier to catch a stray or misplaced key during review, and because adding real constraints (@NotBlank, @Min, etc.) turns a genuinely missing or invalid value into a loud startup failure instead of a silent, permanent fallback.

misconceptions.description: Any class annotated @ConfigurationProperties is automatically registered as a bean and starts binding configuration immediately, the same way @Component works.
misconceptions.clarification: @ConfigurationProperties by itself is only metadata describing what prefix a class should bind to and how -- it is not a stereotype annotation, and it does not, on its own, make Spring register the class as a bean. The class still needs to become a bean through some other mechanism: @Component on the class itself (if it's otherwise reachable by component scanning), @EnableConfigurationProperties(SomeProperties.class) declared on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class. Skip all three, and the class simply never gets bound to anything -- every field quietly reflects whatever default value was hardcoded in the Java class itself, with no error anywhere to reveal that binding never actually happened.

exercises.prompt: A developer sets app.payment.provider=stripe and app.payment.timeout-seconds=10 in application.properties, but PaymentProperties always reports the Java-level defaults ("none" and 5) no matter what the file says. Find and fix the bug.
hints: @ConfigurationProperties alone only describes HOW a class should bind, if it ever becomes a bean at all -- is PaymentProperties actually registered as a bean anywhere here?
Compare this to @Component: without some registration mechanism, does Spring Data JPA-style automatic discovery apply to @ConfigurationProperties the same way?

Add @Component to the class, or @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class -- any one of the three fixes this.
exercises.solutionExplanation: PaymentProperties was never registered as a Spring bean at all -- @ConfigurationProperties only describes the prefix and binding shape for a class IF that class becomes a bean through some other mechanism, and none was present here, so Spring never constructed it, never bound anything to it, and the values hardcoded as Java field defaults ("none" and 5) were the only values that ever existed on any instance. Adding @Component makes PaymentProperties discoverable by ordinary component scanning, which registers it as a bean; once it IS a bean, Spring Boot's configuration-properties binding machinery actually runs against it, reading app.payment.provider and app.payment.timeout-seconds from the Environment and overwriting the Java defaults with the real configured values. @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class, would each independently fix the same underlying problem -- the class simply needs to become a bean by one of these routes before binding can happen at all.

exercises.prompt: Given this class and these two application.properties scenarios, what happens when the application starts in each case?
hints: Notice there is no default value supplied in the ${...} placeholder -- what does @Value do differently when a property genuinely has no default AND no default exists to fall back on?
In Scenario A, the property exists somewhere in the Environment -- resolution succeeds normally.
In Scenario B, the Environment has no value at all for app.reports.cron-expression, and there's no colon-separated default in the placeholder to fall back on.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Scenario A starts normally, with cronExpression bound to '0 0 * * * *'. Scenario B fails to start with IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'app.reports.cron-expression', because the property has no value anywhere in the Environment and the @Value expression supplies no default to fall back on.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The placeholder ${app.reports.cron-expression} has no colon-separated default value written into it, which specifically means Spring has no fallback to use if the real property is missing. In Scenario A, app.reports.cron-expression is defined in application.properties, so the Environment resolves it successfully and ReportScheduler is constructed normally with cronExpression set to the configured cron string. In Scenario B, no property source defines that key at all, and because there's no default to fall back to, Spring MVC's placeholder resolution throws IllegalArgumentException while trying to construct ReportScheduler, which fails the entire application startup rather than silently leaving cronExpression as null. This is the fail-fast behavior that only exists for @Value placeholders WITHOUT a default -- adding one (e.g., :0 0 * * * *) would change Scenario B's outcome to a silent, always-used default instead of a startup failure.

assessments.prompt: A team has six related properties, all under the prefix app.email.*, currently injected individually with six separate @Value fields scattered across three different classes. What is the most accurate reason to consolidate them into one @ConfigurationProperties class instead?
options: @Value is being deprecated in favor of @ConfigurationProperties and will eventually stop working.

Grouping related properties into one typed, optionally validated class keeps them together, makes the relationship between them visible in one place, and can fail fast at startup on missing or invalid values in a way six scattered @Value fields don't provide by default.
@ConfigurationProperties resolves properties faster at runtime than @Value does.
@Value can only inject String values, so numeric or boolean configuration requires @ConfigurationProperties.
assessments.explanation: The real advantages of consolidating into @ConfigurationProperties are structural: one class documents the full shape of a related configuration group in one place instead of six independent injection points scattered across unrelated classes, and adding @Validated with constraint annotations gives a fail-fast startup check that six separate @Value fields have no equivalent for. Option A is false -- @Value remains fully supported and is entirely appropriate for genuinely standalone properties; this isn't a deprecation. Option C is false -- there's no meaningful runtime performance difference between the two for ordinary configuration reads. Option D is false -- @Value can and does resolve to numeric, boolean, and other simply-convertible types, not just String.

assessments.prompt: A developer defaults to @Value for every single configuration value, arguing it's simpler and requires less code than defining a whole @ConfigurationProperties class. Explain when that's a reasonable choice and when it starts to break down.
assessments.modelAnswer: For a single, genuinely standalone property -- one value that isn't part of a larger related group and doesn't need validation beyond basic type conversion -- @Value really is the simpler, more proportionate choice: one annotation, one placeholder expression, done, with no separate class to define or register. The tradeoffs start showing up once you have several RELATED properties scattered across @Value fields in different classes: there's no single place that documents 'these six properties all belong to configuring the email subsystem,' so understanding the full shape of that configuration means hunting across however many classes happen to inject pieces of it. It gets worse specifically around missing or mistyped keys: a @Value field with a default silently falls back to that default forever if the real property is ever typo'd or omitted, with zero signal that anything is wrong, because as far as Spring's placeholder resolution is concerned, nothing failed -- the default mechanism is working exactly as designed. A grouped @ConfigurationProperties class fixes both problems at once: all six related properties live as fields on one class, under one prefix, which is itself a form of documentation, and adding @Validated with constraint annotations turns a missing-or-invalid configured value into a loud application-startup failure instead of a silent fallback. The line I'd draw in practice is: reach for @Value for a handful of genuinely independent, simple properties; reach for @ConfigurationProperties the moment you have a cohesive GROUP of related settings, or the moment a misconfigured value would cause a real production problem that's worth catching at startup rather than discovering later.

concepts.title: Spring Profiles and Externalized Configuration
concepts.description: Profiles let a single build artifact swap in different beans and property overlays per environment through @Profile and application-{profile}.properties, and externalizing configuration -- keeping secrets and environment-specific values out of the files you commit -- is what makes that same artifact safely deployable from local development through production without rebuilding it or leaking a credential into source control.
learningObjectives: Activate a Spring profile via spring.profiles.active and explain how application-{profile}.properties layers on top of, rather than replaces, application.properties.
Use @Profile on a @Bean or @Component to conditionally include or exclude it from the context depending on which profile is active.
Predict what happens when zero, one, or more than one @Profile-guarded bean of the same type is eligible under the currently active profiles.
Explain why hardcoding environment-specific values and secrets directly into application.properties and committing them to source control is a serious, hard-to-reverse mistake.
Explain the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle and how profiles combined with externalized configuration make one build artifact deployable across every environment without recompilation.
Predict the effect of activating two profiles simultaneously with overlapping properties or overlapping @Profile beans.

sections.heading: Activating Profiles and Layered Property Files
sections.body:
A **profile** is a named label -- `dev`, `staging`, `prod`, or anything else you choose -- that you activate at startup via the property `spring.profiles.active`, set through any of the same sources covered in the precedence concept earlier in this module: a command-line argument (`--spring.profiles.active=prod`), an environment variable (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`, following the exact same relaxed-binding rules already covered), or, less commonly for a value that's meant to vary per deployment, directly in `application.properties`.

Once a profile is active, Spring Boot looks for a file named `application-{profile}.properties` (or `.yml`) -- `application-prod.properties`, for `prod` -- and, if it exists, loads it **in addition to** the base `application.properties`, not instead of it. Properties defined only in the base file remain in effect; properties defined in both files take the profile-specific file's value, because profile-specific files rank above the base file in the precedence order already established earlier in this module. This layering, not replacement, is exactly what lets `application.properties` hold every setting that's genuinely the same everywhere, while `application-prod.properties` holds only the handful of values that actually differ for production -- a connection pool size, a log level, a feature flag -- without duplicating everything else.

sections.heading: @Profile on Beans: Swapping Implementations by Environment
Multiple Active Profiles and Property Merging
sections.body:
`spring.profiles.active` can list more than one profile, comma-separated: `spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics`. Each active profile contributes its own `application-{profile}.properties` overlay, and where two active profiles' files define the same key, the later one in the list takes precedence over the earlier one -- so profile ordering in that list is not purely cosmetic. This is a genuinely useful feature for composing orthogonal concerns (`prod` for the bulk of production settings, `metrics` for turning on a separate monitoring integration that isn't specific to any one environment) rather than needing a dedicated `prod-with-metrics` profile for every combination you might ever want.

It's also exactly the mechanism behind the ambiguous-bean scenario from the previous section: if a deployment script activates `dev,prod` together -- through a copy-paste mistake, a misconfigured CI variable, or simply forgetting that profiles compose -- both `@Profile("dev")` and `@Profile("prod")` beans of the same type become simultaneously eligible, and Spring refuses to guess between them. This is worth treating as a real, easy-to-make operational mistake rather than a purely theoretical edge case; keeping mutually-exclusive environment profiles (`dev`, `staging`, `prod`) genuinely mutually exclusive in deployment tooling -- never activated together -- is a discipline worth enforcing deliberately, precisely because Spring itself won't stop you from combining them until the resulting ambiguity actually surfaces at startup.

sections.heading: Externalizing Configuration: Why Secrets Don't Belong in application.properties
sections.body:
Hardcoding a real database password or third-party API key directly into `application.properties` (or a profile-specific overlay) and committing it to source control is a mistake with a genuinely different risk profile from an ordinary bug: git history is, by default, permanent and widely accessible -- deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from history, anyone with clone access (including CI systems, contractors, and, if the repository is ever made public or forked, a far wider audience than originally intended) can retrieve it from an earlier revision indefinitely, and rotating a leaked credential after the fact is genuinely disruptive compared to simply never having leaked it. It also quietly breaks the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle covered next, since a file with production secrets baked in either has to be different from the file used in every other environment (forcing environment-specific builds again) or, worse, means development and CI environments have literal access to production credentials the moment they check out the repository.

The fix follows directly from the precedence and relaxed-binding mechanisms already covered in this module: keep `application.properties` and any profile overlay free of actual secrets, referencing them only as a placeholder with **no default** -- `spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}` -- and supply the real value at deploy time through a strictly higher-precedence source that never gets committed to source control: an environment variable injected by the container platform, a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets), or a dedicated configuration server. Because that placeholder has no default, a deployment that forgets to supply `DB_PASSWORD` fails fast at startup with an unresolved-placeholder error, exactly like the `@Value` example earlier in this module, rather than silently starting up with a missing or blank credential.

sections.heading: Build Once, Promote Everywhere
sections.body: Put together, profiles and externalized configuration are what let a team build exactly **one** artifact -- one jar, one container image, tested once and never rebuilt for a different environment -- and promote that identical artifact through dev, staging, and production, with each environment supplying its own profile activation and its own externally-injected secrets and environment-specific values at the moment it actually runs. This matters for reasons beyond convenience: an artifact that's rebuilt separately per environment can subtly differ between the version that was tested in staging and the version that actually ships to production (a different dependency resolution, a different compiler flag, a different baked-in value), which undermines the entire point of testing in staging in the first place -- you're no longer verifying the artifact that will run in production, only one that resembles it. Building once and promoting the same, unchanged binary forward, with environment differences supplied entirely through profile activation and externally-injected configuration, is what actually closes that gap.

examples.title: Layered Base and Profile-Specific Property Files
examples.code:
# application.properties (base -- applies everywhere)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none
app.notifications.channel=email

# application-prod.properties (overlay -- only when prod is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db.internal:5432/orders
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
examples.explanation: With spring.profiles.active=prod, spring.datasource.url resolves to the production overlay's value -- the profile-specific file wins for any key both files define. spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none and app.notifications.channel=email, defined ONLY in the base file, remain fully in effect under the prod profile too, since application-prod.properties is loaded as an ADDITION to the base file, not a wholesale replacement of it -- there was never any need to repeat every base setting inside the prod overlay just to keep them active. spring.jpa.show-sql=false, present only in the prod overlay, simply has no base-file counterpart to override at all; it's a setting that only exists, and only matters, under this one profile.

examples.title: Swapping a Bean Implementation With @Profile
examples.explanation: Any @Service depending on Notifier through its constructor never needs to know which of these two implementations it actually received -- with dev active, component scanning registers only LoggingNotifier as eligible for the Notifier type, so injection resolves to it unambiguously; with prod active, only SesNotifier is eligible instead. This gives a genuinely safe way to develop and test locally without accidentally sending real emails through a production email provider -- the swap happens purely based on which profile is active, with zero changes to any class that actually depends on Notifier.

examples.title: Externalizing a Database Password Instead of Hardcoding It
examples.code:
# application.properties -- committed to source control, contains NO real secret
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

# Deployment: the container's environment supplies the real value
# DB_PASSWORD=<retrieved from a secrets manager at deploy time, never committed anywhere>
#
# If DB_PASSWORD is missing entirely at startup:
# IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'DB_PASSWORD'
# -- the application fails to start rather than connecting with a blank password.
examples.explanation: The committed application.properties file contains a placeholder, ${DB_PASSWORD}, with no default value -- the actual password never appears anywhere in the repository or its history, because it's never written into any file that gets committed at all. At deploy time, the real value is supplied through a higher-precedence source -- here, an environment variable populated from a secrets manager -- which the Environment resolves the placeholder against, exactly like the relaxed-binding and precedence mechanisms covered earlier in this module. Because there's no default for this specific placeholder, a deployment that forgets to supply DB_PASSWORD fails immediately and loudly at startup instead of silently attempting to connect with an empty or missing credential -- the same fail-fast pattern as a required, default-less @Value placeholder.

misconceptions.description: application-prod.properties replaces application.properties entirely when the prod profile is active -- only the values in the profile-specific file are actually used.
misconceptions.clarification: Profile-specific files are loaded as a layered OVERLAY on top of the base application.properties, not a full replacement of it. Any key defined only in the base file remains fully in effect under any active profile; a profile-specific file only needs to define the handful of keys that genuinely differ for that environment. Only keys that are defined in BOTH files have their base-file value overridden by the profile-specific one -- everything else in the base file is untouched and still applies.

misconceptions.description: It's fine to commit real production secrets into application.properties as long as the repository itself is private.
misconceptions.clarification: A private repository still typically grants access to CI/CD systems, every current team member and contractor, and often a build/audit trail that retains history indefinitely -- and once a secret is committed, deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from git history, where it remains retrievable by anyone who can access any earlier revision. 'Private' also doesn't protect against the repository later being made public, forked, or migrated, at which point a secret committed months or years earlier becomes exposed retroactively. The standard fix -- externalizing secrets through environment variables or a secrets manager, referenced only via a no-default placeholder in the committed file -- means there is simply no secret value present in the repository at any point for any of these scenarios to expose in the first place.

exercises.prompt: Given these two files and spring.profiles.active=prod, what are the final effective values of spring.jpa.show-sql, app.max-upload-mb, and app.support-email once the application starts?
exercises.code:
# application.properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
app.max-upload-mb=10
app.support-email=support@example.com

# application-prod.properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
app.max-upload-mb=25
hints: application-prod.properties is loaded IN ADDITION to application.properties, not as a full replacement of it -- which keys does it actually redefine here?
For any key defined in BOTH files, the profile-specific file's value wins. For a key defined in ONLY the base file, there's nothing to override it with.
app.support-email never appears in application-prod.properties at all -- what happens to a base-file value that the profile overlay simply doesn't mention?
exercises.expectedAnswer: spring.jpa.show-sql resolves to false (overridden by the prod file), app.max-upload-mb resolves to 25 (overridden by the prod file), and app.support-email resolves to support@example.com (defined only in the base file, and therefore untouched and still in effect, since the prod file never mentions it at all).
exercises.solutionExplanation: application-prod.properties is loaded as a layered overlay on top of application.properties, not a wholesale replacement -- so every key present in the base file remains in effect unless the profile-specific file also defines that same key. spring.jpa.show-sql and app.max-upload-mb are both defined in application-prod.properties, so their profile-specific values (false and 25) take precedence over the base file's (true and 10). app.support-email has no entry anywhere in application-prod.properties at all, so there's nothing to override its base-file value with -- it resolves to support@example.com exactly as defined in the base file, completely unaffected by which profile is active.

exercises.prompt: A CI pipeline's integration test step sets `spring.profiles.active=dev,prod` (a leftover from a copy-pasted deployment script) and the application now fails to start with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException for the Notifier type. Given the beans below, explain the bug and fix the CI configuration.
hints: spring.profiles.active accepts a comma-separated list -- what does activating BOTH dev and prod at once do to which @Profile beans are eligible for injection?
LoggingNotifier and SesNotifier both implement Notifier -- if both of their guarding profiles are active simultaneously, are they both eligible for the same injection point at once?
The fix isn't in the Java code at all -- the two beans and their @Profile annotations are correct. Fix the CI environment variable so only ONE of dev or prod is active for this test run.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Corrected CI environment variable -- activate exactly one profile for this test run:
# SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev
exercises.solutionExplanation: With SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev,prod, both dev and prod are simultaneously active, which makes BOTH @Profile("dev") LoggingNotifier and @Profile("prod") SesNotifier eligible for registration at the same time -- both implement Notifier, and with no @Primary or @Qualifier to disambiguate between them, Spring cannot decide which one to inject wherever a Notifier is required, so it refuses to start the application with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, naming both conflicting beans. The Java code and its @Profile annotations are correct as written; they were specifically designed to be mutually exclusive, environment-specific alternatives, not beans meant to coexist. The actual bug is the leftover CI configuration activating both profiles together -- correcting SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE to name only dev (the profile actually appropriate for an integration test run) resolves the ambiguity, since only LoggingNotifier's guarding profile is active at that point.

assessments.prompt: spring.profiles.active=staging is set, and both application.properties and application-staging.properties exist, each defining a value for app.log-level (among other keys). What best describes how the final configuration is assembled?
options: application-staging.properties completely replaces application.properties -- only its values are used at all.

application-staging.properties is loaded as an overlay on top of application.properties; for app.log-level specifically the staging file's value wins, but any key defined only in the base file remains in effect.
Spring Boot merges the two files by keeping whichever value appears first alphabetically by key.
Having the same key in both files causes a startup error, since profile-specific files must not duplicate base-file keys.
assessments.explanation: Profile-specific files layer on top of the base application.properties rather than replacing it outright -- keys defined only in the base file remain fully in effect, and for keys defined in both, the profile-specific file's value takes precedence because it ranks higher in Spring Boot's property source precedence order. Option A is wrong because it describes full replacement, not layering. Option C describes behavior Spring Boot does not implement at all -- there's no alphabetical merge rule. Option D is wrong -- defining the same key in both a base and profile-specific file is completely normal and is, in fact, the entire mechanism by which profile-specific overrides work; it causes no error whatsoever.

assessments.prompt: A team currently maintains three separately-built jars -- one per environment -- each with its own hardcoded database credentials baked into application.properties before every deployment. Explain, using profiles and externalized configuration, how to move to a single build artifact promoted across all three environments, and why that's a meaningfully better practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core problem with three separately-built jars is that the artifact tested in staging is never literally the artifact that reaches production -- each environment gets its own build, with its own baked-in database credentials and environment-specific settings, so a difference introduced during any one of those three separate build steps (a dependency resolving slightly differently, a configuration value typo'd only in the production build) can silently diverge from what was actually verified earlier in the pipeline, undermining the entire point of testing in staging first. Hardcoding real credentials into each build's application.properties compounds this: those secrets end up committed to source control (or baked into a build artifact) at least once per environment, creating a permanent, hard-to-rotate exposure risk that has nothing to do with whether the repository is technically 'private.' The fix is to build exactly one artifact and promote that unchanged binary through dev, staging, and production, letting environment differences come entirely from two mechanisms external to the build itself. First, Spring profiles: keep application.properties limited to settings that are genuinely the same everywhere, and let a small, non-secret application-{profile}.properties overlay per environment (dev, staging, prod) supply only the handful of settings that legitimately differ, activated at deploy time via spring.profiles.active rather than baked in at build time. Second, externalized configuration for anything sensitive or deployment-specific: rather than hardcoding a database password into any properties file, reference it as a placeholder with no default (spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}) and supply the real value through an environment variable or secrets manager at the moment each environment's container actually starts -- a source that's never part of the build and never committed to source control at all. With both pieces in place, the exact same jar, unchanged, behaves correctly in each environment purely based on which profile is activated and which secrets are injected into its environment at runtime -- eliminating both the artifact-divergence risk of separate builds and the permanent leak risk of committed credentials, while also meaning a credential rotation is now an infrastructure-level change, not a rebuild-and-redeploy of the application itself.
